transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Moreno (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (Sandstone, Head of MLOps), Marco Rinaldi (Platform Eng Lead), Tanya Nguyen (Security Architect), Peter Lee (CTO)

Summary (auto): Quick intro, gather constraints for Dedicated pool. Confirm isolation requirements and burst strategy. Agree next steps for pilot and documentation share.

[00:00] Jamie: All right, thanks everyone for joining, um, appreciate the time. Quick round-robin - I'm Jamie Chen, AE at Redwood, and Luis is our SE. Luis, want to say hi?
[00:12] Luis: Hey everyone, hi, Luis Moreno, I own performance and infra for Redwood's Dedicated offering, happy to dig into the details.
[00:18] Aisha: Hi, Aisha here. We're evaluating a Dedicated setup because we have sensitive data and predictable peak trading windows.
[00:24] Marco: Marco, platform eng. I run our GPU infra and orchestration.
[00:27] Tanya: Tanya, security. I'll be triaging compliance controls.
[00:30] Peter: Peter, CTO, I'll mostly listen but want to understand risk and costs.

[00:35] Jamie: Great. Goal today — understand workload (latency/throughput), isolation needs, burst and autoscale expectations, and any compliance must-haves. We'll surface how Redwood Dedicated maps to those and outline a pilot.

[01:02] Aisha: Quick context. We're a quant shop; models are LLM-based pipelines for anomaly detection and trade summarization. Production calls spike around market open and economic releases, so we need reserved capacity plus burst. Target p95 latency under 400ms for short seq gen (256 tokens) and throughput of ~120 qps at peak.

[01:35] Luis: That's helpful. Two clarifying q's: are those 120 qps concurrently persistent or very short bursts? And do you need absolute isolation (single-tenant GPU pools) or is logical isolation in a VPC okay?
[01:47] Aisha: Bursts last 5-8 minutes but can be repeated. We prefer single-tenant for data isolation, and we'd like control over the model image / quantization profile.

[02:05] Marco: Also, we do model caching — we use prefix caching for repeated prompts, and have a KV cache layer; curious how Redwood handles K V cache sharing or sticky routing for hot keys.

[02:18] Luis: Redwood Dedicated supports physical GPU pools dedicated per customer. You can pin model versions and have control plane in your VPC for Private mode; for Dedicated we can do a private tenancy option that gives dedicated instances with customer network isolation. KV cache is local to the serving node by default but we have options for shared redis-backed cache or sticky routing to keep KV hot on the same instance. There might be a tradeoff between perfect isolation and shared cache efficiency.

[02:46] Tanya: On encryption and keys — we require KMS with customer-managed keys, and full audit logs for token-level access. SOC2 attestation is required, plus data residency in US-East for this workload. Can Redwood support CMK and region pinning?

[03:05] Jamie: Yes — we support KMS/HSM integrations and can enable CMKs for Dedicated and Private deployments. We also provide audit logs and can scope retention for enterprise tiers. I'll attach the SOC2 and security pack after the call.

[03:22] Marco: For scaling, how does Redwood handle autoscaling for Dedicated pools? We need predictable latency when autoscaling from reserved capacity to burst nodes — ideally sub-30s spin-up or pre-warmed burst.

[03:34] Luis: Good question. Dedicated supports reserved baseline pools for predictable throughput; we also support burst capacity which is either on the same tenant (pre-provisioned) or cross-region fallback. Spin-up depends on VM image cold start and model loading — with pre-warmed instances we've seen sub-20s for warm images, cold loads can be 60-120s for large GG-like models unless you use sharding + async pre-load. We recommend warm pool for market open bursts.

[04:05] Aisha: So recommendation would be baseline reserved GPUs sized for 60-70% of peak, and pre-warmed burst nodes for the rest?

[04:10] Luis: Exactly. That minimizes cost while hitting latency SLOs. Also intelligent batching and prefix caching reduce per-token cost. For very low-latency paths we offer inference-optimized kernels and quantized model variants; we'll show tradeoffs in the pilot.

[04:30] Peter: What about model updates and rollouts? During rollouts we can't have regressions.

[04:35] Luis: We provide canary rollouts by traffic split, A/B evaluation hooks, and automatic fallback to previous model variants. For Dedicated we'll do staged deploys and keep KV cache warming strategies to avoid cold-start regressions.

[04:50] Tanya: Audit and access control — do you integrate with SSO/SAML and support RBAC so we can separate AE dev teams from prod infra? Also need immutable logs for audits.

[04:58] Jamie: Yes SSO/SAML, SCIM provisioning, and RBAC. Logs are stored in your controlled bucket if required and we can integrate with SIEM.

[05:10] Marco: Let's get a bit more specific on model sizes: our current models are LLaMA-2 13B tuned and a smaller 3B for summaries. We expect the 13B to be the main cost driver. Any recommendations on quantization and performance expectations?

[05:24] Luis: 13B on A100-style hardware with 16-bit or 4-bit quant achieves good latency. We support q4_0 and q2_k Quant variants; typical p95 for 256 tokens on a 13B quantized profile on a single GPU is ~200-350ms depending on batch. We'll include benchmark numbers in the runbook. Also model parallelism can help if you need higher throughput.

[05:50] Aisha: We care about reproducibility of latency numbers — can you run a benchmark with our prompt set and traffic profile?

[05:56] Luis: Absolutely. Proposed pilot: 2-week Dedicated trial with reserved baseline (X GPUs) + pre-warmed burst nodes. We run controlled load tests with your prompt set, measure p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, and failure modes. We'll also test KV cache hit rates and autoscale transitions.

[06:15] Jamie: For pricing, we'll share a Dedicated pricing sheet and SOW. There's a base monthly reserved fee and a burst/overage model. We'll include options for pre-warmed reserved burst nodes vs ephemeral cloud burst.

[06:30] Tanya: A quick security nit: we require all images scanned and signed. Are images you run for Dedicated signed and do you support customer's signed image registry?

[06:40] Luis: Yes, we support customer-provided images hosted in your registry, and we can enforce image signing and scanning policies. For hosted images we perform scanning and can share SBOMs.

[06:55] Marco: How do we handle model artifact storage and versioning? We have an internal model registry.

[07:02] Luis: We can integrate with your model registry or host artifacts in your S3 bucket. Redwood's serving layer supports model pinning and versions. We'll coordinate access controls.

[07:18] Aisha: Are there any known limitations around TF models or only PyTorch? We have some TF export variants.

[07:25] Luis: We primarily optimize for PyTorch and ONNX, but we support TensorFlow models via conversion; we should test your TF artifacts in the pilot.

[07:38] Jamie: Let's capture some numbers: Aisha said p95 target <400ms for 256 tokens at 120 qps peak. Does that map to ~X GPUs reserved? Marco, any current infra baseline?

[07:50] Marco: Right now we run 4x A100-ish nodes for non-LLM batch work, but not tuned for low-latency serving. We were thinking reserved 6 GPUs for baseline and 4 pre-warmed burst for peak, but that's a guess.

[08:05] Luis: Based on rough back-of-envelope, depending on batching and quantization, 6 dedicated GPUs might handle ~60-80 qps with low latencies. To hit 120 qps at p95<400ms you'd probably want 10-12 GPUs (or fewer with model sharding + larger instance types). We'll run proper benchmarks with your load to size accurately.

[08:30] Peter: Cost sensitivity: what's the delta between reserved vs pay-as-you-go burst? We need to present that to finance.

[08:38] Jamie: Reserved capacity is cheaper on a per-GPU-hour basis. Burst/overage has a premium but gives flexibility. We'll provide a cost model with examples based on the pilot results.

[08:50] Aisha: A few questions from ops: network egress, VPC peering, and control plane access. We need control plane in our VPC for some workloads.

[08:58] Luis: We can operate a customer-managed control plane in your VPC for private mode; Dedicated hosted options can also offer private networking and peered VPCs. Egress is billable as usual and can be reduced with model caching and locality.

[09:12] Tanya: Regarding logs and auditing, can we get token-level cost and latency breakdowns per request?

[09:18] Jamie: Yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, latency, and per-route dashboards. We can also forward logs to your SIEM.

[09:28] Marco: On the operational side, what SLAs do Dedicated customers get for latency and uptime?

[09:34] Jamie: SLA commitments are part of Dedicated contracts. Uptime SLAs are available on Reserved plans; latency SLOs are collaborative and tied to configuration (baseline size, pre-warm). We'll define SLOs in the SOW.

[09:50] Aisha: Ok, sounds good. Anything else on security?

[09:55] Tanya: Just need to review the SOC2 and encryption implementation details. Also want to ensure the pilot environment will reflect production networking and KMS.

[10:07] Luis: We'll mirror production as much as possible for the pilot, include CMK usage and run the same network peering. Note some enterprise features require an enterprise contract but we can enable trial-level access for evaluation.

[10:25] Jamie: Great — quick recap and next steps. Action owners: Luis to run benchmark plan; Jamie to send pricing/SOW and security pack; Aisha to provide prompts and target load; Tanya to share compliance checklist. We'll schedule the pilot kickoff next week.

[10:42] Aisha: Timeline looks good — can we get the pricing and SOW by Monday?

[10:46] Jamie: Yes, I'll send the docs by EOD Monday.

[10:50] Marco: One more technical: for KV cache durability, is the cache ephemeral or can we persist hot prefixes across node restarts?

[10:58] Luis: We have options: local in-memory KV (lowest latency) or Redis-persisted KV for durability. Persisted caches add a small latency but survive restarts and help with cold-starts. We'll test both in the pilot.

[11:15] Peter: Sounds good. Any competitor questions? Marco, you flagged Anthropic and CloudVendorAI earlier.

[11:22] Marco: Competitors we've evaluated offer simpler endpoints but not the same ops guarantees. Main reasons to pick Redwood are Dedicated/reserved pools + observability.

[11:30] Jamie: Perfect. We'll follow up with the benchmark plan and security docs. Thanks everyone.

[11:35] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: some technical terms slightly garbled (e.g., K V vs KV cache), proper nouns sometimes mis-typed.
